title: California’s Tallest and Most Iconic Trees Are Getting Heatstroke
summary:
A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests.
This means trees are slowing their “breathing” and “eating” because they can’t cool down fast enough when temperatures rise.
Trees use the pores in their leaves, stomata, to do two things: take carbon dioxide in, and let water out.
Open stomata mean the tree is “breathing” in carbon dioxide and photosynthesizing, but probably also letting water out.
Closed stomata mean the tree is conserving water but also slowing down its photosynthesis, since it isn’t taking in any carbon dioxide.

title: UK launches flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
summary:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.
"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.
Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.
It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.
The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

title: Appeal for major energy storage system in Devon rejected
summary:
Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed.
Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year.
The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire.
A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external.
Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway.

title: Here's How US Recycling Companies Are Turning Old Wind Turbine Blades Into Cement
summary:
Wind turbines are great for generating clean energy, but they have a life cycle of, at most, around 20–30 years.
However, wind turbine blades aren't easy to recycle, as they are made from fiberglass, a material that is difficult and expensive to break down.
Fortunately, recycling companies have found a variety of ways to recycle around 85% of a wind turbine blade, one of which is turning it into concrete and cement.
By breaking down turbine blades, it's possible to recover materials and fibers that are useful for concrete production.
A study published in 2024 concluded that fibers from wind turbine blades can strengthen concrete.

title: Oil theft is on the rise in the heart of U.S. shale country—and it’s mostly carried out in targeted, organized heists
summary:
The spike in oil prices since the Iran war began this year has attracted more thieves, and they are increasingly professional criminals.
While oil theft has long been a part of the industry, the problem has become prevalent enough for the Dallas Fed to ask about in its quarterly surveys.
And now that U.S. oil prices have been hovering around $100 a barrel lately, criminals can't resist the payoff.
Nearly half of the oil executives (47%) said the most common form of theft was targeted and organized, while 42% described it as opportunistic petty theft.
In August, executives from a wastewater disposal company were charged with felony oil theft, money laundering, and organized crime.
